Feb. 4, 1937.
Dear Family:
Flying from Shanghai to Hongkong.
We had to wait at Shanghai for two hours account of heavy fog on the
river at our first port of call - Wenchow.
The first hundred miles
south of Shanghai is over flat country densely populated alluvial
delta land cross laced by innumerable small canals which serve alike
for transportation and for irrigation.
This country is all cultivated
is only rice,
a once a year crop in this section.
fields are bare and brown
new one not yet planted.
for the old crop has been harvested
We have just flown over Ningpo, important
treaty port open to foreign trade, famous for its sailors, missionaries
and Ningpo varnish which is used extensively by furniture
which when not properly dried will give tender skins a rash much like
poison ivy.
In Shanghai the pidgin English for "South" is "Ningpo more
far" which means any point below Ningpo.
As we fly "Ningpo more far"
the brown rice fields give way to low rolling country part rice and
part tea.
The tea bushes are planted in little terraced plots of
ground up
the mountainsides and from the air it is usually hard to
distinguish the rice land from
tea but at this time of year the tea
bushes remain green while the rice fielas are bare.
As we fly farther
South the mountains rise up to 4000 feet, jagged, sawtooth peaks cut
by mountain streams which erode great canyons through the tree-less
unprotected mountainsides, filling up with soil from the hillsides
narrow valleys which are
cultivated closely.
While forest volunteers
have attempted to recapture the mountains which once were theirs, the
Chinese peasants, for some reason unknown to me, light fires and
off all scrub timber even though no use is made
of the burnt over land.
Possibly they gather the charcoat or maybe they find protection against
bandits is improved by the elimination of cover - but whatever the
reason it seems almost criminal.
Messrs. Trippe and Whitney who have flown pretty much every-
where both said
that the scenic beauty of the flight from Hongkong to
Shanghai surpassed any they had seen elsewhere.
Great masses of stone,
narrow canyons cut from the solid rock, five hundred foot high
moss like hills and this
morning the valleys filled
in spots with fog the color of dirty cotton floating as though poured
the valleys by the Gods.
Here we are flying at 5000 feet in a
sunlit sky - no clouds, only
an Arizona blue in the dome from horizon
to horizon yet our last weather report from Wenchow reports
"ceiling
200 meters."
If the fog does not move out of our way - or there are
no holes through which we can fly down to land on the river, we shall
pass up Wenchow and continue on to Foochow.
We have just flown over Fenghua a small town where our aman
Ising Tzu came from and possibly more entitled to fame as the home of
Chiang Kai-shek, whose private airport lies below us.
The Generalissimo
is now there recuperating from his harrowing experiences at Sian-fu.
It is said on good authority that after his imprisonment at Sian-fu
he refused to confer with his captor Chang Hsueh-liang but quietly said
"You are my subordinate and will take orders from me, otherwise you are
a rebel and must shoot me - there is nothing else to be considered and
no reason for conferences."
Chiang Kai-shek is proud, fearless, ruth-
less yet patient.
He has given his life to the unification of China-
an almost,
if not entirely,
impossible task.
How heart sick, disillusion
ed and altogether miserable he must have been, caged, humiliated, and
bullied by a big headed, swashbuckling subordinate who was actuated by
motives almost wholly selfish.

player will sacrifice the right of individual action for the sake of

so many hundreds of generations that it will take many Chiang Kai-sheks
to convert them to a real
and lasting nationalistic spirit.
afraid that Chiang Kai-shek or any other "spear head"
National idea will eventually be undermined, repudiated and denounced,
if not actually murdered, by selfish leaders who seek power and money;
men whose hot heads are controlled even now only by cold feet.
There are evidences of the betterment of law and order every-
That is hopeful.
City walls pulled down to permit the new
highways to enter and leave, good roads building everywhere, improved
radio communication, etc.
Just now we flew over a sugar
loaf shaped mountain on the
which a wall had been built
close an area of possibly four acres.
In the center of the area s
small pond partly full of water.
the precipitous heights of the
sugar loaf zig zag trails from the villages in the peaceful valleys
The zig zag trails seem long neglected as indicated by small
uncleared land slides and thick underbrush covering the several narrow
trails in many places.
In the days when the existence of law and order
was the exception rather than the rule,
the first hint of trouble sent
the natives, like our New England ancestors, scurrying up to the se-
clusion and comparative safety of this natural large scale "block house!
the impenetrable strength of which was assured by the precipitous cliffs
on all sides.
The era which sees these strongholds go to rack and
ruin while concurrently the temples and historic shrines are being re-
paired and reconstructed is truly an important one and there is hope
yet for China.
I used to think that Chiang Kai-shek with the backing of a world
recognized National Government, a small
but well equipped loyal army,
plus money and control of the Chinese Air Force could rule all China.
The Chinese aviators are mostly American trained and fly American
planes but they are still Chinese with the same ideas and objectives
as their fellow countrymen.
With a few exceptions,
very few, they can
be expected to act like any other Chinese military
or political leaders.
Arriving at Wenchow the fog had happily moved out and the sun
was shining brightly.
In the lee of the small station house the deck
of the barge was still wet evidencing the accuracy of our previous
weather reports.
Now as I write we have left Wenchow, Foochow and Amoy and are
headed for Swatow.
I have just counted 22 separate and distinct forest
fires - obviously
not accidental as they are too far apart to have
caught fire from a spark.
Just makes me sick to see it.
This country
here is about like the mountains round about Lake George - only not a
tree - just low scrub which will undoubtedly be burned before it can
get far up the mountainside.
Now below is another "block house" with
the wall fallen down on one side and no trails
foot of the hill runs the modern highway which leads from Amoy to
Swatow.
I have just been looking over my "log", a little book in which
are entered all flights,
and find that this is
my twenty-seventh trip
on the 1000 miles route between Shanghai and the South, Canton or Hong-
Its about an eight hour flight as against two days and nights on
We have
just left Swatow, Years ago a French missionary's wife,
who was an expert on needlework,
taught her amah how to do fine embroid-
More Chinese women began to do "French" embroidery and now, as I
think I wrote you once before, the industry is one of China's most im-
portant ones.
Before starting this trip I wrote to a friend in Swatow
and asked him to find me a "Spanish" shawl, most all of which come from
Just now when we taxied up to the
float I saw our agent with a
bundle under his arm and a letter from my friend sending a shawl with
his compliments.
Haven't opened the box but hope it is a good one. Also
have a little Ming blanc de chine eight sided cup for Debby and a drawing
book for Cat.
Don't know how I'll square myself with Hebe unless I have
a chance to make a purchase on the way home. Approaching Hongkong.
As ever,
